paragraphs: Metformin is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients 10 years of age and older with type 2 diabetes [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-2]. In a U.S. clinical trial of metformin hydrochloride tablets in patients with type 2 diabetes, a total of 141 patients received metformin hydrochloride tablets up to 2550 mg per day, and adverse reactions reported in greater than 5% of treated patients and more common than placebo included diarrhea (53% vs 12%), nausea/vomiting (26% vs 8%), flatulence (12% vs 6%), asthenia (9% vs 6%), indigestion (7% vs 4%), abdominal discomfort (6% vs 5%), and headache (6% vs 5%) [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-2]. In placebo-controlled trials of metformin hydrochloride extended-release tablets, 781 patients were administered the drug, and adverse reactions reported in greater than 5% of patients and more common than placebo included diarrhea (10% vs 3%) and nausea/vomiting (7% vs 2%) [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-3].

The sources do not provide a direct comparison of metformin's efficacy against other treatments for type 2 diabetes. One registry entry describes a study of rimonabant added to metformin and a sulfonylurea, but it does not report the results of that comparison [ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT00546325]. Another registry entry describes a study of a prebiotic product added to metformin, but it does not report the results of that comparison [ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT05689684]. A review discusses clonal hematopoiesis and type 2 diabetes, noting that preclinical studies found metformin might slow clonal expansion, but it does not provide clinical evidence of this effect in people [PubMed:42374733].

The FDA label lists serious warnings for metformin, including lactic acidosis, vitamin B12 deficiency, and hypoglycemia [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-2, openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-3]. In clinical trials of 29-week duration, a decrease to subnormal levels of previously normal serum vitamin B12 levels was observed in approximately 7% of patients [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-2]. Postmarketing reports have identified cholestatic, hepatocellular, and mixed hepatocellular liver injury, but these reactions are reported voluntarily from a population of uncertain size, making it difficult to reliably estimate their frequency or establish causality [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-3].

The sources do not provide information on the long-term effects of metformin on complications such as cardiovascular disease or microvascular complications. A review notes that clonal hematopoiesis is associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and that metformin might slow clonal expansion, but it does not provide clinical evidence of this effect in people [PubMed:42374733]. The sources also do not provide information on the use of metformin in specific populations, such as those with prediabetes or those living in neighborhoods with high socioeconomic disadvantage. One study analyzed the relationship between neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage and the use of diabetes prevention interventions, but it did not focus on metformin alone [PubMed:42377443].

The sources do not provide information on the use of metformin in pediatric patients. The FDA label indicates that metformin hydrochloride tablets are indicated for pediatric patients 10 years of age and older, but it does not provide details on the safety or efficacy of metformin in this population [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-2]. The sources also do not provide information on the use of metformin in patients with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) type 5. One case report describes a patient with HNF1B-related MODY who maintained excellent metabolic control on metformin alone, but it does not provide generalizable evidence for the use of metformin in this population [PubMed:42369057].
uncertainty: The registry entries for the rimonabant and prebiotic studies do not report the results of the comparisons, so the sources do not provide efficacy data for metformin in those specific combinations [ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT00546325, ClinicalTrials.gov:NCT05689684].

The review on clonal hematopoiesis and type 2 diabetes reports preclinical findings that metformin might slow clonal expansion, but it does not provide clinical evidence of this effect in people [PubMed:42374733].

The sources do not provide information on the long-term effects of metformin on complications such as cardiovascular disease or microvascular complications, and the postmarketing reports of liver injury are not reliable for establishing frequency or causality [openFDA label:FDA-LABEL-metformin-3].

stages.uncertainty_review: All three uncertainty items checked against complete context. Supplied registry excerpts contain plans and no measured efficacy results; uptake study is not treatment-effect evidence, so no-direct-efficacy-comparison is valid. Preclinical CH limitation is supported. No established metformin effect on CVD/microvascular complications is supplied. Spontaneous liver reports cannot estimate frequency/causality, correctly preserved. The mixed third item cites the liver label for a broader all-source long-term gap; adjacency is weak but not an invented outcome.
